summary: Digests the user-network interface of NTT Communications' dual-stack ADSL service, which gives home users both IPv6 and IPv4. It focuses on two parameters, the prefix assigned to the user and the IPv6 DNS server addresses, and describes how they are delivered automatically to customer premises equipment. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you plug in a home router, it should figure out its internet settings by itself. This memo describes how one provider did that for the new kind of internet address.

questions: how does isp give ipv6 prefix to home router
how does home router get ipv6 address block
dual stack ipv6 ipv4 home network
subtitle: How home routers automatically configure IPv6 on dual-stack internet connections.

tldr.problem: Home users need both IPv4 and IPv6 internet, but manually configuring IPv6 parameters is complex and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: The system automatically assigns each home router an IPv6 prefix via DHCPv6, delivers DNS server addresses, and handles IPv6 setup alongside IPv4 over a single PPP connection.
tldr.outcome: NTT Communications deployed this in 2002, proving that dual-stack home access could work with zero user configuration.

today: RFC 4241 is an Informational RFC that documents a production system NTT Communications deployed in 2002. It remains a practical reference for ISPs implementing dual-stack home access with automatic IPv6 configuration.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Users have always needed to set up their internet connections. IPv4 requires fewer parameters, but IPv6 adds complexity: an ISP must assign each home a prefix (a block of addresses to use) and tell the devices where to find IPv6 DNS servers.

This RFC documents a practical system used by NTT Communications since 2002 that solves this problem. Instead of asking users to type in IPv6 settings, the system discovers and configures everything automatically when you plug in.

The system works over ADSL with a Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) connection. The ISP side, called the Provider Edge (PE), talks to the home router, called Customer Premises Equipment (CPE), through this link.
sections.eli5: When you plug in your router, it should already know everything it needs without asking you any questions. This memo explains how an ISP can set that up for IPv6.

sections.title: The Network Setup
sections.content:
The system runs two independent negotiation protocols on a single PPP link: one for IPv4 (IPCP) and one for IPv6 (IPV6CP). They work at the same time without interfering with each other, so a user can have only IPv4, only IPv6, or both.

The architecture focuses on PPP and the layers above it. ADSL line details are left to the access layer below. The ISP assigns each customer a /48 prefix (the RFC prefers this size to leave room for future needs), though /64 is also possible.

After initial PPP setup, the router needs two things from the ISP: the IPv6 prefix to use on its home network, and the addresses of IPv6 DNS servers. The system delivers both automatically using DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: Both IPv4 and IPv6 travel down the same wire at the same time, but they do not bother each other. The ISP sends your router a large block of addresses and a list of name servers to use.

sections.title: Assigning Addresses Automatically
sections.content:
When the router powers on, it negotiates with the ISP using DHCPv6. The router asks for a prefix (IA_PD option), and the ISP chooses one from an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) server or a local pool.

The ISP replies with an IA_PD option containing the prefix length (48 bits in this system). The router then subnets that prefix into smaller /64 blocks and assigns one to each of its connections (its upstream link and each home network interface).

Once the router has a prefix, it begins sending router advertisements on each home network, telling devices they can use addresses from the assigned /64. The home devices then automatically assign themselves global IPv6 addresses using the stateless autoconfiguration process from RFC 2462.
sections.eli5: The ISP hands your router a block of addresses like 2001:db8:ffff::/48. Your router then breaks it into smaller pieces (like 2001:db8:ffff:1::/64 for the kitchen and 2001:db8:ffff:2::/64 for the living room), and tells your devices they can use those.

sections.title: DNS Servers and Routing
sections.content:
During the same DHCPv6 exchange where the router requests a prefix, the ISP notifies the router of recursive DNS server addresses using the DNS Configuration option (RFC 3646). The router can pass these addresses to its home devices in router advertisements, or act as a DNS proxy itself, like a home IPv4 router does today.

Routing between the home and ISP is static: the router uses the ISP link as its default gateway. If the router receives a packet destined for an address within its delegated /48 that was not assigned to any home interface, it discards the packet or sends an ICMPv6 error. This prevents packets from leaking to the ISP for addresses the home does not actually use.
sections.eli5: The ISP tells your router where to send DNS queries (like 8.8.8.8 for IPv4). Your router can pass this address to home devices, or pretend to be a DNS server itself. Any address your home network is not using goes straight to the recycle bin.

sections.title: Bringing It All Together
sections.content:
When a router first plugs in, a specific sequence of steps happens. First, PPPoE discovery establishes the connection. Then PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP) negotiates the PPP layer itself. PPP authentication using CHAP follows, proving the router is allowed to connect. After that, IPv4 Control Protocol (IPCP) sets up IPv4, and IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP) sets up IPv6. Finally, DHCPv6 gives the router its prefix and DNS servers.

IPv4 and IPv6 can be used as soon as their respective protocol negotiation completes. IPv6 with link-local addresses (the fe80:: range) becomes available after IPV6CP. Global IPv6 becomes available after prefix delegation completes. This allows IPv4 and IPv6 to be independent: if IPv6 fails, IPv4 still works, and vice versa.
sections.eli5: Plugging in the router triggers a chain of conversations: discovery, connection setup, login, then IPv4 configuration, then IPv6 configuration. Each step unlocks what you can do: you get IPv4 quickly, then IPv6 comes later.
